export const meta = {
  name: 'phase1-1beyond-cmc-extractor',
  description: 'Analyze 1 Beyond DLLs and the SIMPL .cmc, and build a Crestron .pkg extractor with tests',
  phases: [
    { title: 'Work', detail: 'build pkg_dump.py; analyze 1 Beyond i20/p20 DLLs, the .cmc format, and Automate VX three-way' },
    { title: 'Verify', detail: 'adversarial check per analysis dimension' },
    { title: 'Synthesize', detail: 'what these samples change about the project' },
  ],
}

const R = '/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert'

const GROUND = `
PROJECT: ${R} — research into converting AV control-system device drivers between vendors.

ESTABLISHED BY DIRECT INSPECTION (trust; do not re-derive):

EXTRON
- .pkp = gzip over a .NET BinaryFormatter (NRBF) stream, unencrypted/unsigned. Working parser:
  'python3 ${R}/tools/pkp_dump.py <file.pkp> -o out.json'
- It embeds one Python driver per transport as StreamResourceAsset byte arrays, written against
  the Global Configurator runtime (Extron2.BaseDriver / Extron2.HTTPDriver), delimited by
  '### BEGIN AUTO GENERATION OF COMMAND DEF' ... '### END'.
- Multi-transport packages appear as N_models x N_transports DriverModelAssets, each owning ONE
  ProtocolAsset child (SerialProtocolAsset or EthernetProtocolAsset) plus its own
  _scriptFileName/_scriptClassName.
- The separately shipped ControlScript module is a different Python dialect over 'extronlib'
  (class DeviceClass, a self.Commands dict, AddMatchString regexes, transport mixin classes).

CRESTRON
- .pkg = plain ZIP. Typically <name>.dat (a JSON capability manifest) + <name>.dll. IR packages
  have no DLL (.ir + .dat + .pdf).
- In the Samsung QN43LS03DAFXZA samples the DLL was a ~16 KB shell: 2 TypeDefs, ONE MethodDef,
  zero fields, a 22-byte ctor doing ldarg.0 / ldtoken / call Type.GetTypeFromHandle / ldstr
  <resourceName> / call base-ctor / ret, inheriting
  Crestron.DeviceDrivers.Core.LegacyWrappers.DisplayWrapperSerial (or DisplayWrapperTcp).
  The real driver was plain uncompressed UTF-8 JSON stored as a CLR ManifestResource: raw bytes
  in .text behind a 4-byte little-endian length prefix, NOT inside a metadata heap.
  In the Serial DLL that was file offset 0x1068, length 0xb454 = 46,164 bytes, starting with a
  UTF-8 BOM.
- That JSON is a rule-engine DSL with sections SchemaVersion / GeneralInformation / UserAttributes
  / Transports / SupportedFeatures / CommandIds / Commands / Responses / Conditions /
  Transformations / Rules / Controllers / InputOutput. It matches the public 'DriverDefinition'
  class in Crestron's API reference property-for-property.
- Crestron's SDK has two documented architectures: V1 (RAD Framework, JSON + a compiled C#
  protocol class inheriting ABaseDeviceProtocol) and V2 (Entity Model, from SDK 21.x, data-driven
  via a DriverController). Neither is deprecated; SDK v28 shipped 2026-04-28. The LegacyWrappers
  JSON-engine form is a third path Crestron's tutorials never document.
- Load path has NO signing or certification gate. The DLLs are Authenticode-signed with a
  self-signed cert and are NOT strong-name signed; nothing checks it.

THE NEW SAMPLES (this is your subject):
  "${R}/samples/Automate VX/Controlscript/onebynd_sm_Automate_VX_Series_v1_0_11_0.py"  (+ .pdf)
  "${R}/samples/Automate VX/pkp/1bynd_42_4279_v1_0_11.pkp"                              (+ .pdf)
  "${R}/samples/Automate VX/Crestron Module/1Beyond Automate_VX_v1.2.cmc"               (+ .pdf)
  "${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-i12_i20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.pkg"
  "${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-p12_p20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-P20_IP.pkg"
  (each .pkg also pre-extracted into a sibling directory of the same name)

FIRST OBSERVATIONS (unverified, challenge them):
- The 1 Beyond camera DLLs are 145,080 bytes — nearly 10x the Samsung shell — with the embedded
  JSON marker '"SchemaVersion"' found at offset 22,981, and NEITHER 'LegacyWrappers' NOR
  'Crestron.RAD' appearing anywhere in the file. The .dat reports sdkVersion 23.0000.0000,
  developer "Crestron", deviceTypeId "Unknown".
- The .cmc is plain ASCII with CRLF line endings and an ini-like block structure
  ('[', 'ObjTp=FSgntr', 'Sgntr=CresMacro', 'RelVrs=4.30.01', 'ObjTp=Hd', 'PrNm=...').
- 1 Beyond is a Crestron-owned brand, so Automate VX is the MIRROR of the earlier Samsung case:
  Crestron-branded hardware with an Extron driver.

RULES:
- Cite path:line, JSON path, or byte offset for EVERY claim. No citation, no finding.
- NEVER submit placeholder or test content. If you cannot establish something, say so and report
  what you tried. A stub is worse than an honest gap.
- Web access ONLY via the Bright Data CLI ('brightdata search "q"' / 'brightdata scrape <url>').
  Never WebFetch/WebSearch, never curl to target sites — the owner's home IP must not be used.
- Structured output must be valid JSON: no angle brackets, no XML-ish tags, no unescaped
  backslashes (use forward slashes), no raw newlines inside strings.
- FILE WRITES: only the pkg-extractor agent may write under ${R}/tools/. Everyone else works in
  /tmp. Nobody else writes anywhere in the repo.
`

const FIND = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    summary: { type: 'string' },
    findings: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          evidence: { type: 'string' },
          confidence: { type: 'string', enum: ['high', 'medium', 'low'] },
          implication: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'evidence', 'confidence'],
      },
    },
    openQuestions: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'summary', 'findings'],
}

const VERD = {
  type: 'object',
  properties: {
    dimension: { type: 'string' },
    verified: {
      type: 'array',
      items: {
        type: 'object',
        properties: {
          claim: { type: 'string' },
          verdict: { type: 'string', enum: ['CONFIRMED', 'REFUTED', 'UNCERTAIN', 'OVERSTATED'] },
          note: { type: 'string' },
        },
        required: ['claim', 'verdict'],
      },
    },
    missedOrWrong: { type: 'array', items: { type: 'string' } },
  },
  required: ['dimension', 'verified'],
}

const DIMS = [
  {
    key: 'oneb-i20-dll',
    prompt: `THE MOST IMPORTANT QUESTION IN THIS PHASE. Determine whether the 1 Beyond IV-CAM-I20 IP
driver carries REAL COMPILED LOGIC or is another JSON-engine shell.

File: "${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-i12_i20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.dll" (145,080 bytes).

Do a full PE/CLI metadata analysis. Write a Python reader if no tool is installed (try monodis,
ikdasm, ilspycmd first; a #~ / #Strings heap reader in Python is entirely feasible as a fallback).
Report:
- The complete TypeDef and MethodDef name lists, with counts. Samsung had 2 TypeDefs / 1 MethodDef.
- Every AssemblyRef with version and PublicKeyToken (Samsung referenced .NET Compact Framework
  mscorlib 3.5.0.0, token 969db8053d3322ac).
- All ManifestResource entries: name, offset, size. Extract the embedded JSON and report its exact
  byte length and top-level section list.
- ACCOUNT FOR THE FILE. 145,080 bytes total, JSON marker at ~22,981. How many bytes are IL method
  bodies, how many are metadata, how many are the resource, how many are PE overhead? If there is
  substantial IL, DISASSEMBLE the largest methods and describe what they do — do they build command
  strings and parse responses (i.e. real device logic), or are they framework plumbing?
- What base class does the driver type inherit? If not LegacyWrappers, what is it, and does it
  correspond to SDK V1 (RAD, ABaseDeviceProtocol/ADeviceTypeProtocol) or V2 (Entity Model,
  DriverController, [EntityCommand] attributes)?
- Is it Authenticode-signed? Strong-name signed?

THE VERDICT TO REACH: is 100% of this driver's behaviour recoverable from declarative data, or is
some behaviour only in IL? If the latter, quantify how much and what kind. This decides whether
"Crestron in" generalises across the catalogue or only covers the JSON-engine subset.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'oneb-p20-dll',
    prompt: `Do the same full PE/CLI analysis for the 1 Beyond IV-CAM-P20 IP driver:
"${R}/samples/Crestron 1 Beyond IV-CAM-p12_p20/Crestron/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-P20_IP/Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-P20_IP.dll"

Report the same items as the I20 analysis: TypeDef/MethodDef lists and counts, AssemblyRefs with
versions and PublicKeyTokens, ManifestResource entries with offsets and sizes, extracted JSON with
its section list, a full byte-budget accounting of the file, the base class and which SDK
architecture it implies, and signing status.

Then DIFF I20 against P20. The i12/i20 and p12/p20 are different camera families (the P series is
Crestron's PTZ line, the I series is the intelligent/auto-tracking line — verify rather than assume).
Establish: are the two DLLs the same shell with different JSON, the same code with different data,
or genuinely different implementations? Compare their IL method sets and their JSON.

If the two are near-identical apart from data, that is strong evidence for a reusable engine even
without LegacyWrappers. If they differ substantially in IL, that is evidence of per-device compiled
logic and is the bad case for the project.

Also compare BOTH against the Samsung shells: what changed between Samsung's SDK 21 LegacyWrappers
shell and these SDK 23 drivers?`,
  },
  {
    key: 'cmc-format',
    prompt: `Reverse-engineer the Crestron SIMPL macro format from
"${R}/samples/Automate VX/Crestron Module/1Beyond Automate_VX_v1.2.cmc" (59,033 bytes, ASCII, CRLF).

It has an ini-like block structure: bracketed blocks containing KEY=VALUE lines, with keys like
ObjTp (object type), Sgntr, RelVrs, IntStrVrs, MinSMWVrs, SavedBy, S0Nd/S1Nd/SLNd, PrNm, DbVr, DvcDbVr.

Fully characterise it:
- Enumerate every distinct ObjTp value and what each block kind represents.
- Work out the graph structure: how are blocks linked (the Nd / node fields look like a linked
  structure — establish how). SIMPL is a dataflow language, so there should be symbols and signals.
- Identify how SIGNALS (digital / analog / serial joins) are declared and named, and how symbols
  reference them.
- Find whether any device COMMAND STRINGS appear anywhere in the file — literal serial/TCP payloads
  the macro sends to the Automate VX. This is the decisive question: is a .cmc a source of protocol
  knowledge at all, or purely wiring between other symbols?
- Determine whether any part is compiled/opaque (SIMPL+ blocks are sometimes embedded and may be
  password-protected or binary).
- Use 'brightdata search'/'scrape' for any public documentation of the SIMPL file format, the
  community SMW/UMC format notes, or Crestron KB article id-3358.

CONCLUDE: finding 04 ruled the SIMPL family out as "program logic, not a driver". Is that ruling
CORRECT for this file? Argue it from the file's actual contents, and say specifically what a
converter could and could not recover from a .cmc.`,
  },
  {
    key: 'automate-vx-three-way',
    prompt: `Automate VX is the MIRROR of the Samsung case: Crestron-branded hardware (1 Beyond is
Crestron-owned) with an EXTRON driver. Do the three-way comparison.

Sources:
  A) Extron ControlScript: "${R}/samples/Automate VX/Controlscript/onebynd_sm_Automate_VX_Series_v1_0_11_0.py"
  B) Extron .pkp:          "${R}/samples/Automate VX/pkp/1bynd_42_4279_v1_0_11.pkp"
     Parse with: python3 ${R}/tools/pkp_dump.py "<the .pkp>" -o /tmp/avx.json
     Extract every StreamResourceAsset script.
  C) Crestron .cmc:        "${R}/samples/Automate VX/Crestron Module/1Beyond Automate_VX_v1.2.cmc"

Establish:
1. What transport(s) does the .pkp carry? How many DriverModelAssets, and what ProtocolAsset does
   each own? Does the ControlScript module derive from one of the embedded scripts, and what is the
   verbatim line-overlap percentage (stripped and exact) plus the AddMatchString regex match count?
2. What protocol does Automate VX actually speak? Extract the wire strings from the Extron side.
   Is it a text protocol, JSON, HTTP/REST, something else?
3. Do any of those wire strings appear in the .cmc? Answer concretely — this is the empirical test
   of whether a SIMPL macro carries protocol knowledge.
4. Compare the capability sets: what can the Extron driver do, what can the Crestron macro do?

The Samsung case established that two vendors independently encoding the same DOCUMENTED protocol
converge byte-for-byte, including on its bugs. This case tests something different: a vendor
encoding ANOTHER vendor's hardware, where the manufacturer is Crestron itself. Report whether the
convergence result reproduces here or breaks, and what that means for the general claim.`,
  },
]

phase('Work')
log('Phase 1: 1 Beyond DLL analysis, SIMPL .cmc reverse-engineering, Automate VX three-way, plus building the .pkg extractor')

// The extractor build runs concurrently with the analyses; only it writes to the repo.
const extractorP = agent(
  `${GROUND}\n\nYOUR TASK: build a Crestron .pkg extractor, the counterpart to the existing
tools/pkp_dump.py. Write it to ${R}/tools/pkg_dump.py. You are the ONLY agent permitted to write
under ${R}/tools/.

WORK TEST-FIRST. Write ${R}/tools/test_pkg_dump.py alongside it, and make the tests fail before
they pass. Use pytest if available, else a plain 'python3 test_pkg_dump.py' runner with asserts —
check what is installed and adapt rather than assuming.

The tool must:
- Take a .pkg path (or a directory of them) and unzip it in memory.
- Parse the outer .dat capability manifest as JSON.
- For packages with a DLL: locate and extract the embedded driver-definition JSON from the CLR
  ManifestResource. Do NOT hardcode offset 0x1068 — that was one file. Parse the PE headers, find
  the CLI header (IMAGE_COR20_HEADER) via the COM descriptor data directory, read the Resources
  RVA/size, walk the ManifestResource table in the #~ metadata heap, and resolve each resource's
  offset properly, reading the 4-byte little-endian length prefix. Strip a UTF-8 BOM if present.
  Fall back to a brace-matched '"SchemaVersion"' scan ONLY if metadata parsing fails, and say so
  in the output.
- For IR packages with no DLL: handle them gracefully, emitting the .dat and noting the .ir file.
- Emit a normalised JSON document per package: manifest, driver definition, member inventory with
  sizes, and a 'notes' list recording anything unusual or any fallback used.
- Provide a --summary mode printing one line per package: name, members, resource size, driver JSON
  section counts.
- FAIL LOUDLY on anything unexpected. Never silently return partial data.

Validate against ALL FIVE Crestron packages in the repo (3 Samsung: Serial, IP, IR; 2 1 Beyond:
I20, P20). The Samsung Serial resource must come out at exactly 46,164 bytes and the IP one at
80,889 bytes (both including the BOM) — treat those as regression assertions.

Report what you built, the test results (actual output, not a claim), and any package that
defeated it.`,
  { label: 'build:pkg_dump', phase: 'Work', model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
)

const analysed = await pipeline(
  DIMS,
  (d) => agent(`${GROUND}\n\nYOUR DIMENSION: ${d.key}\n\n${d.prompt}`, {
    label: `analyze:${d.key}`, phase: 'Work', schema: FIND, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high',
  }),
  (res, d) => {
    if (!res) return null
    return agent(
      `${GROUND}\n\nYou are an adversarial verifier for "${d.key}". REFUTE the findings below rather than ` +
      `agreeing. Reproduce each claim against the actual files yourself. CONFIRMED only if you personally ` +
      `reproduced it. REFUTED if contradicted. OVERSTATED if directionally right but claimed too strongly. ` +
      `UNCERTAIN if uncheckable.\n\nBe most skeptical of: byte-budget accounting (recount it), any claim ` +
      `that IL is or is not "real logic" (disassemble and judge for yourself), percentages (recompute), and ` +
      `any claim about what a .cmc does or does not contain (grep the file yourself).\n\n` +
      `If the researcher submitted placeholder or test content, say so explicitly in missedOrWrong.\n\n` +
      `Their brief:\n${d.prompt}\n\nFINDINGS:\n${JSON.stringify(res, null, 2)}`,
      { label: `verify:${d.key}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERD, model: 'sonnet', effort: 'high' }
    ).then((v) => ({ dimension: d.key, analysis: res, verification: v }))
  }
)

const extractor = await extractorP
const dossier = analysed.filter(Boolean)
const counts = dossier.reduce((a, d) => {
  for (const v of (d.verification && d.verification.verified) || []) a[v.verdict] = (a[v.verdict] || 0) + 1
  return a
}, {})
log(`Phase 1 analysis done: ${dossier.length}/${DIMS.length} — ${JSON.stringify(counts)}`)

phase('Synthesize')
const synthesis = await agent(
  `${GROUND}\n\nVerified dossier from 4 dimensions plus the extractor build report follows.\n\n` +
  `Write the synthesis. Treat REFUTED as false, OVERSTATED as weaker, UNCERTAIN as unproven.\n\n` +
  `Answer, in order:\n` +
  `1. Do the 1 Beyond drivers carry real compiled logic? State the answer plainly and quantify it. ` +
  `Then say what it means for "Crestron in": does it generalise across the catalogue, or only over ` +
  `the JSON-engine subset? If the latter, how would a tool DETECT which kind a package is, and what ` +
  `should it do when it meets the hard kind?\n` +
  `2. Is a .cmc usable as a source of protocol knowledge? Confirm or overturn the earlier ruling that ` +
  `the SIMPL family is program logic rather than driver data. Say specifically what is recoverable.\n` +
  `3. What did Automate VX show — does the cross-vendor convergence result reproduce when the ` +
  `hardware vendor IS the other control-system vendor?\n` +
  `4. What these three samples change about the project's plan, concretely. Include anything that ` +
  `should be revised in findings 02 through 06.\n` +
  `5. The single highest-value thing to do next, and why.\n\n` +
  `Prose with headings, minimal bullets, cite evidence. Do not pad. Do not hedge where evidence is ` +
  `clear; do not overclaim where it is not. The reader is an AV professional who writes code.\n\n` +
  `EXTRACTOR BUILD REPORT:\n${extractor}\n\nDOSSIER:\n${JSON.stringify(dossier, null, 2)}`,
  { label: 'synthesis:phase1', phase: 'Synthesize', model: 'opus', effort: 'high' }
)

return { dimensions: dossier.length, verdictCounts: counts, extractor, dossier, synthesis }

## Summary

Built `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/tools/pkg_dump.py`, the Crestron `.pkg` counterpart to `pkp_dump.py`, plus `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/tools/test_pkg_dump.py` (23 tests, plain-assert runner — pytest is not installed in this environment, checked first with `python3 -c "import pytest"`, which failed). Confirmed the tests failed before the tool existed (`ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'pkg_dump'`) before writing `pkg_dump.py`.

**How the extractor works** (no hardcoded offsets): a from-scratch minimal PE32/PE32+ reader (`PEImage`) walks DOS/COFF/optional headers to the data-directory array, reads the COM-descriptor (CLI header / `IMAGE_COR20_HEADER`) via directory entry 14, resolves its Metadata and Resources RVAs to file offsets through the section table, parses the `BSJB` metadata root and its stream headers, then a full ECMA-335 `#~` tables-stream reader (`TablesStream`) — with real column/coded-index definitions for all 45 standard metadata tables — walks table row-blocks in ascending table-id order up to `ManifestResource`, decodes its `Offset`/`Name`/`Implementation` columns, and reads the 4-byte length-prefixed payload at `ResourcesFileOffset + Offset`. A UTF-8 BOM is stripped only for JSON parsing; `raw_bytes`/`size` in the output still include it. If PE/metadata parsing fails for any reason, it falls back to a proper brace-matched (string/escape-aware) scan for `"SchemaVersion"` and records that fact in `notes`; if both paths fail, it raises `DriverExtractionError` rather than returning partial data.

**Test results (actual output)**:
```
23 passed, 0 failed, 23 total
```
Byte-exact regressions verified: Samsung Serial resource = 46164 bytes (incl. BOM), Samsung IP = 80889 bytes (incl. BOM) — both matching the numbers given in the task.

**Validated against all 5 real Crestron `.pkg` samples** via `python3 tools/pkg_dump.py samples --summary`:
```
Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.pkg      members=2 resource_size=116874 method=cli-metadata driver_sections=11
Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-P20_IP.pkg      members=2 resource_size=109648 method=cli-metadata driver_sections=11
FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_IP.pkg      members=2 resource_size=80889  method=cli-metadata driver_sections=14
FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_IR.pkg      members=3 no-dll                driver_sections=0
FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.pkg  members=2 resource_size=46164  method=cli-metadata driver_sections=13
```
No package defeated the metadata parser — the brace-matched fallback path was never needed for real samples (only exercised in tests via a deliberately corrupted COM-descriptor RVA). Cross-checked the two 1 Beyond resource-start offsets against the known raw-string marker offsets from the task brief (22981 for I20, and 20681 for P20, both `marker_offset == resource_start_offset + 1`, i.e. the payload's very first byte is `{`) — confirmed exact match, proving the metadata-table walk lands on the right bytes rather than coincidentally close ones.

One real finding, noted in the tool's output: the 1 Beyond camera driver JSON top-level sections (`SchemaVersion, GeneralInformation, ConfigurationSteps, Transports, Commands, Responses, Conditions, Transformations, Rules, Controllers, DriverController`) differ from the Samsung display driver JSON's sections (`... UserAttributes, SupportedFeatures, CommandIds, ... InputOutput` per the established facts, and confirmed here — Samsung has 13/14 sections including `driverId`/`userAttributes` style keys, 1 Beyond has 11 including `ConfigurationSteps`/`DriverController` which Samsung lacks). Both still carry the `"SchemaVersion"` marker and the same rule-engine shape, but the section set is not identical across the two DLLs' embedded schemas — worth flagging for whoever writes the cross-vendor mapping.

Files:
- `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/tools/pkg_dump.py` — the extractor
- `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/tools/test_pkg_dump.py` — the test suite (23 tests)

No files were written anywhere else in the repo; scratch validation scripts were built and removed under `/tmp/pkgwork` and `/tmp/pkg_dump_out`. Nothing was committed to git.

analysis.summary: Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.dll is NOT a JSON-engine shell like the Samsung sample. It is a full Crestron SDK V2 (Entity Model) driver assembly: 36 TypeDefs / 84 MethodDefs / 79 Fields / 133 MemberRefs / 86 TypeRefs, referencing Crestron.DeviceDrivers.EntityModel and Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK v26.0.26.0 (not LegacyWrappers). The 116,874-byte embedded JSON (SchemaVersion 2.0) covers most of the protocol (82 Commands/31 Responses/54 Conditions/26 declarative Transformations/70 Rules/73 Controllers), but 6 of the Transformation names invoked by the JSON's own Rules (FormatRomVersion, ParseDecimal, ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles, ZoomLevelToPosition, ZoomPositionToLevel, ApplyZoomPositionStep) have NO entry in the JSON's declarative Transformations array — their behavior exists only as ~5.9KB of compiled IL in matching TypeDef/Factory classes registered via [ImplementationProviderAttribute]. Verdict: behavior is NOT 100% recoverable from declarative data; a real (if small) slice — binary protocol assembly, table interpolation, and an async scene/camera-view state machine with timeouts — is IL-only.

findings.evidence: AssemblyRef table dump: 'mscorlib 3 969db8053d3322ac', 'System.Core 3 969db8053d3322ac', 'Crestron.DeviceDrivers.EntityModel 26', 'Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK 26' (from /tmp/resolve_check.py-adjacent query on mdtables.AssemblyRef).

findings.claim: The driver's own module Assembly is 'Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP' version 2.100.9.0; the type '.DriverEntity' extends Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK.EntityModel.ReflectedAttributeDriverEntity and '.EntryPoint' extends Crestron.DeviceDrivers.EntityModel.DriverAssemblyEntryPoint - this is SDK V2 (Entity Model), not the Samsung LegacyWrappers path.

analysis.summary: Automate VX does NOT reproduce the Samsung-case convergence pattern. The two Extron dialects (ControlScript source A, and the .pkp-embedded script B) converge heavily because they are literally two Extron in-house rewrites of the SAME Extron-authored driver against the SAME documented 1 Beyond REST/JSON API (identical 32 endpoint strings, verbatim). But the Crestron .cmc (C) is a SIMPL macro/join wrapper with ZERO occurrences of any of those wire strings, JSON field names, the token endpoint, or the auth header pattern. It is not an independent re-encoding of the wire protocol at all -- it is a GUI/join-map shell that delegates the real protocol implementation to a separately-compiled SIMPL+ module (\"1Beyond Automate_VX_v1.2.csp\") referenced by name inside the .cmc but not present in the sample set. So the empirical test this dimension was designed to run cannot complete on the Crestron side at the wire-string level: convergence is confirmed on the Extron-vs-Extron pair, and is untestable (not \"broken\", but \"blocked\" -- the artifact needed is missing) on the Extron-vs-Crestron pair. What IS testable and confirmed is command-level (semantic) parity: every Extron command name/feature (AutoSwitch, CameraPresetRecall, PanTilt/Zoom, Layout A-Z, RoomConfiguration/ForceRoomConfiguration, Scenario, Sleep/Wake, ISORecording, Record, Stream, SwitchCamera, HomeShotPreset/GoHome, Login credentials, IP/Port, HTTP-vs-HTTPS toggle) has a same-named join in the .cmc -- except CameraPresetSave, which has no corresponding join anywhere in the macro.

findings.claim: The .pkp carries exactly ONE transport: Ethernet/HTTP(S). There are 3 DriverModelAssets (Automate VX, Automate VX Pro, Automate VX Plus), and the live model tree contains exactly one EthernetProtocolAsset per model (3 total in the live tree); no SerialProtocolAsset exists anywhere in the package.

Models 110 ('Automate VX Pro', wrapper obj 947 -> item 2970) and 111 ('Automate VX Plus', wrapper obj 950 -> item 2990) resolve to byte-identical EthernetProtocolAsset field values (address/port/subtype/auth all equal). The 4th EthernetProtocolAsset/DanteAsset pair is object 113 (a ClassWithMembersAndTypes acting as the metadata template for AssetBase<IProtocolAsset>), whose AssetBase+_parentAsset ($ref 34) is the generic-wrapper schema object itself, not any of the three DriverModelAssets -- it is a serialization-template artifact of the NRBF metadata declaration, not a fourth live per-model transport.

findings.claim: Automate VX speaks a JSON-over-HTTPS REST protocol: POST requests to paths like 'api/StartRecord', bodies are JSON, auth is a raw (non-Bearer-prefixed) token placed directly in an 'Authorization' header obtained via a POST to 'get-token' with Basic-style base64(username:password) credentials, and it explicitly forces the https scheme.

Token flow: TokenRequestHandler (lines 183-193) POSTs to cmdString='get-token' and stores res['token']. 32 distinct 'api/*' endpoint strings extracted (e.g. 'api/StartRecord','api/StopRecord','api/CallCameraPreset','api/GoHome','api/ForceChangeRoomConfig','api/GoToScenario') -- see /tmp/pkp_endpoints.txt.

findings.evidence: grep over 316 distinct 'Nm=' join names in the .cmc found: AutoSwitch_{Enabled,Disabled}_FB; Call_Live_Camera_Preset / Call_Selected_Camera_Preset (recall only); Camera_{Up,Down,Left,Right,UpLeft,UpRight,DownLeft,DownRight}[_Debounced] and Camera_Zoom_{In,Out}[_Debounced] (PanTilt/Zoom); Change_Layout_A..Z + _FB (Layout); Change_Room_Config/Force_Room_Config/Get_Current_Room_Config/Get_Room_Configs/Number_of_Room_Configs (RoomConfiguration/ForceRoomConfiguration); Recall_Scenario/Current_Scenario/Get_Scenarios/Number_of_Scenarios (Scenario); Sleep/Sleep_FB, Wake/Wake_FB; Start_ISO_Recording/Stop_ISO_Recording/Toggle_ISO_Recording/Get_ISO_Record_Status/ISO_Recording_{Started,Stopped}_FB (ISORecording); Recording_State/Recording_{Started,Stopped}_FB (Record); Stream_{Started,Stopped}_FB (Stream); Manual_Switch_Camera/Manual_Switch_Camera_FB (SwitchCamera); Go_Home/Go_Home_FB (HomeShotPreset); Start_Output/Stop_Output/Toggle_Output/Get_Output_Status/Output_{Started,Stopped}_FB (Output); Login/Login_FB/PersistentLogin/Username$/Password$ (credentials matching the driver's DriverCredentials Username/Password); IP_Address/Hostname$ and Port (connection params). A case-insensitive grep for 'save' across all 316 join names returned zero results -- no Save-Camera-Preset control exists in the macro, while the Extron driver explicitly implements it (_cmd_SetCameraPresetSave, POST 'api/SaveCameraPreset', /tmp/avx_embedded_script.py line ~289).

findings.claim: The macro's fixed camera-control join count (263) is consistent with, and slightly exceeds, the Extron driver's documented camera range of 1-255, suggesting the SIMPL author built per-camera joins up to the device's max (255) plus a handful of fixed system joins.

findings.claim: Where A and B diverge, it's in plumbing/error-text, not protocol semantics -- confirming they are a rewrite pair, not a byte-identical fork: ControlScript (A) builds the HTTPS RootURL directly at construction time and drops the GC framework's Set/Update/Live/Emulated state-machine entirely, while the .pkp script (B) inherits an http-scheme RootURL from the Extron2.HTTPDriver base class and patches it to https via string replace, and retains (but effectively no-ops) a __SafeToSet gate.
findings.evidence: ControlScript source A line 29: "self.RootURL = 'https://{0}:{1}/'.format(ipAddress, port)" (built directly, no base-class involvement). Embedded script B lines 866-867/912-913: "url = '{0}{1}'.format(self.RootURL.replace('http', 'https', 1), url)" -- self.RootURL is never assigned in B (it comes from the Extron2.HTTPDriver base class, defaulting to http:// per the EthernetProtocolAsset's protocolSubType=0/TCP). B additionally defines '__SafeToSet(self, command): return True' (unconditional stub) at line ~857, a vestige of the GC 'Emulated'/'Live' status-tracking framework (self.Commands entries in B carry 'Set'/'Update'/'Live'/'Emulated' keys, e.g. line 105) that A's self.Commands dict (line 34) does not carry at all -- A reimplements connection/status tracking manually via its own OnConnected/OnDisconnected/WriteStatus methods instead.

This is the single missing artifact that would let the convergence-vs-divergence question be answered directly for the Crestron side.

# Synthesis: the 1 Beyond cameras, the .cmc, and Automate VX

## 1. Yes — the 1 Beyond drivers carry real compiled logic, and it is not a rounding error

Stated plainly: these are not shells. The Samsung packages set the baseline for what a shell looks like — `FlatPanelDisplay_Samsung_QN43LS03DAFXZA_Serial.dll` (62,624 bytes inside the .pkg) has **2 TypeDefs and 1 MethodDef**; the IP DLL (99,488 bytes) is identical in shape. `Camera_Crestron-1-Beyond_IV-CAM-I20_IP.dll` (145,080 bytes) has **36 TypeDefs, 84 MethodDefs, 79 Fields, 53 CustomAttributes**; the P20 DLL (135,352 bytes) has **33 / 76 / 76 / 50**. Both reference `Crestron.DeviceDrivers.EntityModel` and `Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK` v26.0.26.0 with no `LegacyWrappers` or `Crestron.RAD` TypeRef anywhere. This is SDK V2 (Entity Model) in the wild — the second architecture the project has now seen first-hand, and the `.dat` manifests agree (`sdkVersion 23.0000.0000` vs Samsung's 14 / 21 / 22).

The compiled slice is small by weight and large by consequence. Total IL across all 84 I20 methods is **5,582 code bytes plus 359 header bytes = 5,941, i.e. 4.1% of the file**, against 116,874 bytes of embedded JSON (80.6%, at file offset `0x59C4`). But bytes are the wrong meter. Three things live outside the JSON:

**Tier 1 — named plugins compiled into the package.** The JSON's Rules invoke transformations by name. I20 references 39 distinct names; **13 have no entry in the JSON's own `Transformations` array**, P20 12 of 39. Seven of I20's orphans resolve to classes in the same DLL, registered by a custom attribute whose blob is literally an interface type name plus a key string — `ITransformationProvider, Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK, Version=26.0.26.0, …, PublicKeyToken=null` followed by a length-prefixed `FormatRomVersion`, `ParseDecimal`, `ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles`, `ZoomLevelToPosition`, `ZoomPositionToLevel`, `ApplyZoomPositionStep`, and `Polynomial`. P20 registers the same set minus `ViscaAssemble2LowerNibbles` — which is also the one name P20's JSON never references. The compiled plugin set tracks each model family's JSON needs; these are per-driver code, not shared boilerplate.

**The `Polynomial` registration is the finding that should change how the ingester is designed.** It is registered for both `ITransformationProvider` and `ITransformInfoTypeProvider` under the *built-in* name. The JSON's two `"Type": "Polynomial"` entries — `ZoomPositionToFieldOfView` and `FieldOfViewToZoomPosition`, carrying only `Min`/`Max`/`MinInput`/`MaxInput` — look completely declarative and are not. Their semantics are supplied by `OverridePolynomialTransformation` IL in the package. A JSON-only importer that implements `Polynomial` per the documented meaning produces a driver that runs, answers, and returns wrong numbers. Silent-wrong, not loud-wrong.

**Tier 2 — calibration data in `.text`.** Both DLLs carry 6 `FieldRVA` rows. In I20, file offset `0x22424` holds 26 doubles `[0, 2256, 4500, 6744, 9744, 12756, …, 31424]` paired with `0x224fc` `[1.0, 1.2, 1.5, 2.0, 3.0, 5.0, …, 188.8]`, and `0x225cc`/`0x226e4` hold a 35-point pair `[1..20, 40, 60, … 320]` / `[0, 6225, 8894, …, 31424]` — two zoom-level↔VISCA-position curves, one per camera model in the family. The strings `2256`, `12756`, `6225`, `10486` appear nowhere in the 116,874-byte JSON. The zoom curve of these cameras is not in the driver definition. It is a static array in the assembly, read by `Calculate`'s `First`/`Last`/`ElementAt` + `ldelem.r8` interpolation.

**Tier 3 — names that resolve inside the SDK, off the package entirely.** The remaining orphans (`Identity` ×23, `Sum`, `Product`, `Subtract`, `Divide`, and notably `ViscaExtractNibbles` ×10 and `ViscaAssemble4LowerNibbles` ×9) have no matching class in either DLL. They must be resolved by `Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK` 26.0.26.0 on the processor. The last two are protocol-shaped, not generic math: VISCA nibble packing is wire semantics living in a shared runtime that ships with neither package.

### What this means for "Crestron in"

It does **not** generalise across the catalogue as a JSON-only problem. But the right correction to finding 04 is not "there are two kinds, one trapped". It is: **one kind, plus a small, enumerable, per-package residue.** The 1 Beyond drivers are still ~96% declarative. What defeats a converter is not the architecture, it is a dozen names.

Detection is cheap and does not need a decompiler. In order of cost:

The `MethodDef` row count in the `#~` stream is a clean binary discriminator today — 1 means shell, 76–84 means code — and `pkg_dump.py` already parses everything needed to read it. Better than a threshold, though, is the actual question: **enumerate every name the JSON references and try to resolve it.** A name is resolvable if it is declared in the JSON's own `Transformations`, or if it appears as an `ImplementationProvider` key in the DLL's CustomAttribute blobs (a plain length-prefixed string, greppable without IL analysis). Anything left over is unresolved. A non-zero `FieldRVA` count is the second flag: static initialised data means behaviour keyed on numbers that are not in the definition. The `.dat` manifest correlates too — both hard packages report `deviceTypeId: "Unknown"` with an empty `features` array against Samsung's real type and 63 features — but N=5, so treat that as a pre-filter, never a decision.

On meeting the hard kind, the tool should convert the declarative part and **quarantine, never drop**. Concretely: any Command, Response or Controller whose transformation chain touches an unresolved name is emitted into a manual-work report with its full chain, not into the output driver. That is finding 04's opaque-flagged-node escape hatch, applied in the Crestron→X direction rather than the Extron→Crestron one. Decompiling to recover the IL is technically easy and strategically wrong: finding 04 already flagged §4.2(c), and independently, IL semantics are not stable across driver versions — you would be re-porting by hand on every vendor release.

## 2. The .cmc: finding 04's ruling stands, and the detail in it needs fixing

Confirmed, and the case is stronger than stated. `/Users/robp/GitHub/rob-paprocki/extron-driver-convert/samples/Automate VX/Crestron Module/1Beyond Automate_VX_v1.2.cmc` is 59,033 bytes of pure ASCII/CRLF — zero non-ASCII bytes in the whole file — arranged as 323 ini-style blocks of 8 kinds (`Sg`=308, `Sm`=8, `Symbol`, `Hd`, `FSgntr`, `Dp`, `Bw`, `Bk`). It contains **no wire protocol at all**: zero double-quote characters, zero `\xNN` escapes, zero CR/LF literals, no `api/`, no `token`, no port numbers. The only `http` in the file is `Lbl1=HTTP` / `Lbl2=HTTPS` at lines 3837/3839 — a dropdown label pair for the `Request_Type` parameter.

The one component that could hold logic is a sub-symbol at line 1771, `Nm=1Beyond Automate_VX_v1.2.csp`, carried as a bare name plus I/O wiring arrays. No `.csp`, `.usp` or `.ush` exists anywhere in the repo. This artifact is not "program logic instead of driver data" — it is an I/O contract plus a dangling pointer to logic that was never shipped. (Note the container/logic separation is established by the file itself, not by Crestron KB id-3358, which the dimension cited: that article covers `.umc`/`.usp`, a different pair.)

**What is recoverable is real, and it is not protocol.** 263 named fixed inputs and 263 named outputs, 308 named signals with types (147 serial `$`-suffixed, 21 analog, 133 implicit digital), grouped by `[~BeginGroup~]`/`[~EndGroup~]` markers into Layouts, Room_Configs, Camera_Controls, Plugins and Scenarios, plus the transport parameter. That is a complete, human-readable capability inventory: usable as a coverage checklist and a test oracle for feature parity, useless as a source of bytes.

That forces one correction to finding 04's artifact table, which describes SIMPL-family modules as having "numbered joins, no named commands". For `.cmc` that is wrong — the joins are named, and the names are the value. Add a `.cmc` row: *Crestron-supplied macro; named joins and a full capability inventory; no wire syntax; protocol logic in a companion `.csp` that ships separately or not at all.* (Also discard the S0Nd/S1Nd/SLNd argument from that dimension: `Sm` blocks with `H=2` and `H=3` do exist, so the stated evidence is false; handles are scoped per object type, not globally.)

## 3. Automate VX: the mirror test did not run

The convergence result does not reproduce, and the honest reason is that it was **blocked, not broken**. Crestron did not ship a Certified Driver for its own Automate VX — it shipped a SIMPL module whose protocol code is absent. There is nothing on the Crestron side to compare bytes against. Meanwhile the two 1 Beyond camera packages *are* real `.pkg` CCDs for Crestron-owned hardware, but no Extron driver for them is in hand. The two new sample sets break the pairing in opposite directions, and neither completes the Samsung experiment.

What did reproduce is one level down: **Extron vs Extron**. The `.pkp` (`1bynd_42_4279_v1_0_11.pkp`) holds 3 DriverModelAssets — Automate VX, Pro, Plus — all pointing at *one* embedded script, `_1bynd_42_4279.py` (47,253 bytes), over a single Ethernet transport at port 4443. That script and the shipped ControlScript module share all 32 `api/*` endpoint strings byte-for-byte plus `get-token`, and 312 of the ControlScript's 527 non-blank lines (59.2%) appear verbatim in the other. Where they differ it is plumbing: the ControlScript builds `https://{ip}:{port}/` directly at line 29, the embedded script inherits an http `RootURL` from `Extron2.HTTPDriver` and patches the scheme with a `.replace('http','https',1)`, and carries a `__SafeToSet` that unconditionally returns `True`.

Command-level parity against the .cmc is near-complete — every Extron command family has a same-named join except `CameraPresetSave`, which has no join anywhere among the 316 names. So the *capability* surfaces agree across vendors; only the encoding is unobservable.

Two caveats worth carrying. First, the 59.2% is an unordered bag-of-lines figure; an order-aware `difflib` ratio on the same two files is ~35.5%, and findings 02 and 06 quote overlap numbers computed by a different method. Pick one method and restate all three. Second, this device speaks JSON over HTTPS against a documented vendor REST API, so even a successful cross-vendor comparison here would have proved much less than Samsung did. The Samsung result was strong because two teams converged on an *undocumented firmware bug* at byte level. Two teams agreeing on `POST /api/StartRecord` is two teams reading the same PDF.

## 4. Concrete revisions to findings 02–06

**Finding 03** — its open question "is the DLL genuinely a thin wrapper, or is behaviour hidden in IL?" is now answered, and the answer is *it depends on the package, not on the vendor*. Record both data points with the discriminator (`MethodDef` = 1 vs 76–84).

**Finding 04** — three changes. Add the `.cmc` row and fix "numbered joins". Rewrite the "three ways a .pkg can be written" section: form 2 (V2 Entity Model) is no longer a documentation abstraction, and its real shape is not "C# methods that send bytes by hand" — it is *the same JSON rule engine plus a handful of `[ImplementationProvider]`-registered plugin classes and static calibration arrays*. Then soften "trapped: drivers written the V1/V2 C# way": V2 packages are ~96% ingestible with a measurable residue, which is a different planning problem from a write-off. N is now 4 non-IR packages across 2 architectures; the catalogue fraction remains unmeasurable.

**Finding 05** — narrow "no decompiler needed" to the LegacyWrappers shell form. For 1 Beyond you either decompile or you lose the zoom curves. And extend "fail loudly on any unknown `Type`" to the thing that actually bites: **unknown or unresolvable transformation *names*, including names that shadow built-in types.** `Polynomial` has a known `Type` and unknown semantics; a Type-only guard sails straight past it.

**Finding 06** — strategy A (in-place resource patch) still holds structurally: `pkg_dump.py`'s metadata walk lands on the 1 Beyond resource at exactly `marker_offset − 1` for both cameras, so it is the same length-prefixed blob in `.text`. But add the constraint that a V2 DLL cannot be repurposed as a generic shell — its plugin classes and `FieldRVA` arrays come along and will be invoked by name. Also adjust the multi-transport rule's worked example: Automate VX is 3 models × 1 transport sharing **one** script, so the model→script mapping is many-to-one and the Samsung "12 models = 6 sizes × 2 transports" count must not be read as one script per model.

**Finding 02** — Automate VX is a third Extron-to-Extron data point and the first HTTP one. It shows the "SIS-specific runtime shell" caveat generalises into a shell *taxonomy*: the converter needs at least three templates (SIS serial, generic match-string, and HTTP request/response with zero `AddMatchString` in either script). For HTTP drivers, acceptance-on-the-wire-string-table becomes acceptance on (method, path, body shape) — the endpoint set is the oracle, and here it matches perfectly.

## 5. The highest-value next step

**Build an unresolved-reference census on top of `pkg_dump.py`, and run it over every `.pkg` in hand.**

For each package: extract the driver JSON, collect every referenced name (transformations first, then Command/Response/Condition `Type` values), and sort it into three buckets — declared in the JSON, registered in the DLL by an `ImplementationProvider` attribute key, or unresolved. Report the unresolved list, the `FieldRVA` static-data inventory, and the `MethodDef` count.

It wins on four counts. It needs no hardware, no portal, no dealer relationship and no decompiler — all four of which gate every other open item. It converts finding 04's central unknown from an opinion into a per-package number, and it is the only method that scales to a catalogue the moment more samples arrive. Its output *is* the converter's quarantine list, so the work is not diagnostic overhead — it is the ingester's front half. And its very first result decides how big the hard problem really is: tier 3 (`Identity`, `Sum`, `ViscaExtractNibbles`, `ViscaAssemble4LowerNibbles`) resolves inside `Crestron.DeviceDrivers.SDK` 26.0.26.0, which finding 04 already established is on public NuGet with no login. If that assembly's built-in transformation vocabulary is readable, tier 3 collapses from "unrecoverable" to a one-time lookup table, and the genuinely hard residue shrinks to per-driver plugins and calibration arrays — six names and four double arrays for I20. That is a tractable manual-work report. Nobody currently knows whether that collapse happens, and it is one afternoon's work to find out.

The alternatives are worse buys right now. The 4-Series load test is gated behind the partner relationship (finding 04's correction on VC-4). The `.csp` acquisition is a single-device answer to a question that only matters for one sample. And an Extron `.pkp` for an IV-CAM camera — which would be the true mirror of Samsung, and would be the biggest scientific prize here — is an acquisition with uncertain success; worth pursuing in parallel, not instead.
